messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Children Present: Being around children, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Carlos Martinez was sixty-seven years old, a prosecutor who had spent four decades in the same courthouse, a man who believed he knew every corridor and every shadow in the building. Two years ago, at a retirement party for a colleague, he had been cornered in a storage room by another prosecutor—a man he had worked beside for years, someone he had called a friend. The party was in a banquet hall off the main lobby; children of several colleagues were running between tables, laughing, while adults talked over drinks. Carlos had gone to the storage room to retrieve an extra chair, and the man followed him inside. What happened there was quick and brutal. The room was cold, air-conditioning vent blowing directly onto his back, and he remembered that precise temperature on his skin—cool, almost clammy—because it became the only thing he could focus on, the only detail that felt real. Afterward, he walked out, made an excuse, and drove home. He never told anyone.

In the weeks that followed, Carlos began to feel as though a film of grime had settled on his skin that no shower could remove. He would stand under hot water for twenty minutes, scrubbing until his arms ached, but the feeling of contamination clung to him. His body, he became certain, had been permanently damaged—a stiffness in his hips, a twinge in his lower back that he had never noticed before, now felt like evidence that something inside had been broken beyond repair. He stopped going to the gym, stopped walking the extra blocks from the parking garage. The world, he started to believe, was a dangerous place, and his own body was no longer a safe vessel.

The memories arrived without warning: the white ceiling tiles, the cold air, the sound of the door clicking shut. They were not memories, really—they happened to him again, right now, in the present tense. He would be standing at the bench in a courtroom, about to deliver a closing argument, and suddenly he was back in that room, the temperature on his skin, the weight of the man, the helplessness. His hand would shake. He would lose his train of thought. He began to notice, as soon as he entered any room—a courtroom, a conference room, even his own office—where the exits were. He counted them. He noted every object that could be used as a weapon: the heavy stapler on the clerk’s desk, the metal legs of a chair, a ballpoint pen held by a juror. He avoided going to unfamiliar places—new courthouses, restaurant chains he hadn’t visited before—because he could not assess the danger in advance. His caseload shrank. He handed off trials that required travel or new venues.

The triggers were everywhere, and they were specific. A certain temperature—the cool air of a courtroom in summer, the chill from a subway grate—could send him spiraling. Being around children made his chest tighten; the laughter that had filled that banquet hall now felt like a threat. And known people—any colleague who resembled the man, any familiar face in the hallway—made him rearrange his schedule, take the stairs, leave the building early. He had become a man who mapped his days around avoidance.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in open court. He was delivering a closing in a domestic violence case—a case that, years ago, he would have argued with righteous certainty. In the gallery, a child of the defendant was sitting with a relative, fidgeting. The air conditioner clicked on, and Carlos felt a cool draft on his neck. He froze. The judge asked if he was all right. He stammered an apology, asked for a recess, and walked out. He sat in the men’s room with his head in his hands, and for the first time he understood that he could not keep doing this on his own. He was terrified that his career—everything he had built—was slipping away. He was also terrified that talking about it would make it worse. But he made the call anyway, not certain what he hoped for, only that he could not continue living inside a memory that refused to stay in the past.
